a: In a new group, I usually take a little time to listen and get a feel for people before becoming involved.
b: In a new group, I usually start connecting with people fairly quickly.

a: Even after a people-heavy day, I often still enjoy talking and interacting with people I like.
b: After a people-heavy day, I usually want quiet time before I feel socially recharged.

a: With unfamiliar people, I usually prefer a few deeper conversations.
b: With unfamiliar people, I am comfortable moving between several conversations and contacts.

a: When I am engaged in a group, I often become quite visible in the discussion.
b: I am comfortable contributing without necessarily being especially visible.

a: I usually wait until there is a clear reason before putting a different view forward.
b: If I see a better approach, I usually put it forward even when the current plan is workable.

a: If a senior person is confident but I see a risk, I am comfortable raising it during the discussion.
b: If a senior person is confident but I see a risk, I prefer gathering my evidence and choosing the right moment before raising it.

a: If a request is inconvenient but manageable, I tend to accommodate it rather than push back.
b: If a request creates a real concern, I usually state the boundary or negotiate it directly.

a: When tension appears with someone, I usually prefer addressing the issue fairly soon.
b: When tension appears with someone, I usually need time to think before discussing it.

a: External deadlines and visible milestones help me keep long projects moving at the right pace.
b: I usually create my own internal pace even when nobody is checking progress.

a: I work best when I can see regular progress or milestones along the way.
b: I can keep pushing steadily even when progress is slow and there is little feedback.

a: When several important things compete for attention, I narrow my focus to protect quality.
b: When several important things compete for attention, I naturally increase pace and try to keep several moving.

a: For a large unfamiliar task, I like enough structure in place before I really begin.
b: For a large unfamiliar task, I am comfortable starting with the next clear action and developing the structure as I go.

a: When the outcome is clear but the method is not, I prefer briefly confirming the approach before starting.
b: When the outcome is clear but the method is not, I am comfortable choosing an approach and getting started.

a: Once I believe I have enough information, I am comfortable committing without checking my decision with someone else.
b: Before an important commitment, I value checking my thinking with someone I trust.

a: After an important decision, I sometimes revisit it to make sure I have not missed something.
b: Unless new information appears, I usually stop reconsidering a decision once I have made it.

a: For a small reversible decision near the edge of my authority, I am comfortable using judgement and updating the relevant person afterwards.
b: For a small reversible decision near the edge of my authority, I would rather check before acting.

a: I can work effectively with files and information arranged in a way that makes sense mainly to me.
b: I prefer files and information arranged consistently enough that another person could find them without me.

a: During busy periods, I prefer maintaining one reliable system for tasks, deadlines and follow-ups.
b: During busy periods, I am comfortable using changing notes and reminders as priorities move.

a: Visual clutter does not bother me much if I know where everything is.
b: I find it easier to work when my physical or digital environment is clearly organised.

a: Even with a familiar process, I prefer a checklist, control or repeatable sequence for important steps.
b: If a repeated process is familiar, I am comfortable relying mainly on experience and judgement.

a: Before sending important work, I focus my checking on the parts most likely to cause problems.
b: Before sending important work, I prefer a consistent checking process even for areas unlikely to be wrong.

a: Once the main outcome is achieved, I prefer closing the associated follow-ups while the matter is still active.
b: Once the main outcome is achieved, I am comfortable batching smaller follow-ups for later.

a: If I discover that my work contributed to a problem, I prefer correcting as much as possible before drawing attention to it.
b: If I discover that my work contributed to a problem, I prefer making the impact and corrective action visible early.

a: When a deadline suddenly moves forward, I reorganise the remaining steps so the essential work and necessary close-out stay controlled.
b: When a deadline suddenly moves forward, I concentrate first on the essential outcome and let secondary administration catch up afterwards.

a: When two explanations seem possible, practical experience usually tells me where to begin.
b: When two explanations seem possible, I prefer checking what evidence would distinguish between them.

a: When strong new information challenges my first conclusion, I am comfortable changing direction fairly quickly.
b: When strong new information challenges my first conclusion, I prefer testing the new information before changing position.

a: When records conflict with what experienced people believe happened, I give considerable weight to their experience.
b: When records conflict with what experienced people believe happened, I usually investigate the records and assumptions before deciding.

a: I usually prefer solving the immediate practical problem before exploring the wider pattern.
b: I often become interested in why the problem happened and whether it points to a wider pattern.

a: If a method is working reliably, I prefer keeping it until there is a clear reason to change.
b: Even when a method works, I tend to notice opportunities to test a better approach.

a: I learn unfamiliar systems best by exploring them and working out the structure as I go.
b: I learn unfamiliar systems best once I understand the rules and structure first.

a: Sudden changes are easier when I can first work out a revised plan.
b: Sudden changes are easier when I start adapting immediately and refine the plan while moving.

a: Even when something has worked for a long time, I can become interested in testing whether a better method now exists.
b: When something has worked for a long time, that history is meaningful evidence for keeping it.

a: When a decision is necessary, I focus first on getting the outcome right and then manage its interpersonal impact.
b: When a decision is necessary, I naturally consider the outcome and interpersonal impact together.

a: When someone is upset about a work issue, I usually begin by understanding their perspective before solving it.
b: When someone is upset about a work issue, I usually begin by clarifying the problem that must be solved.

a: I value communicating consistently so everyone receives essentially the same message.
b: I naturally adjust how I communicate according to the person receiving the message.

a: When a colleague repeatedly struggles, I tend to first become curious about what is driving the difficulty.
b: When a colleague repeatedly struggles, I tend to focus first on what structure or performance change is required.

a: In a disagreement, some issues resolve better after everyone has had time to cool down.
b: In a disagreement, I usually prefer bringing the issue into the open before it has time to grow.

a: If a disagreement can be worked around, I may leave it rather than risk unnecessary tension.
b: If an issue is likely to repeat, I prefer discussing it even if the conversation is uncomfortable.

a: If preserving a relationship requires accepting an outcome that is still workable, I can often do that.
b: If an issue is important enough, I am comfortable risking temporary tension to resolve it properly.

a: In conflict, I prefer a calm, relational framing that makes it easier for the other person to stay engaged.
b: In conflict, I prefer a concise, direct framing so the issue is not diluted.

a: When I am frustrated, people who know me can usually see or hear it.
b: Even when I am frustrated, my outward manner usually changes relatively little.

a: Under uncertainty, I usually focus more strongly on the next thing I can control.
b: Under uncertainty, I naturally think through several ways things could go wrong.

a: When pressure builds, I often feel the emotional intensity even if I continue functioning.
b: When pressure builds, my internal emotional state generally stays relatively steady.

a: When several stressful things happen together, I am usually able to compartmentalise them and deal with them one at a time.
b: When several stressful things happen together, I tend to carry some of that tension between tasks.

a: After a tense interaction, I usually need some processing time before my attention is completely elsewhere.
b: After a tense interaction, I can usually redirect my attention to the next task fairly quickly.

a: I usually extract what is useful from criticism and mentally move on fairly quickly.
b: Criticism from someone whose opinion matters can stay on my mind for a while.

a: After conflict, I usually recover best by getting some space before continuing normally.
b: After conflict, I can usually return to normal interaction without needing much space first.

a: Once I understand how to correct a significant mistake, my confidence usually recovers quite quickly.
b: A significant mistake can affect my confidence for a while even when I know how to correct it.
